Macron vows accountability after France's protests turn deadly, with two dead
items.summary:
President Emmanuel Macron addressed France on Sunday evening after a weekend of protest that slid into some of the worst rioting the country has seen in years. About 550,000 people marched on Saturday, including roughly 110,000 in Paris, in a movement that began with students angry about crumbling schools and the cost of living. By nightfall parts of the demonstrations had turned destructive, and by Sunday the toll included two dead — a 22-year-old police officer struck by a vehicle in Nantes and a protester who suffered a cardiac arrest north of Paris — along with more than 600 injured officers and over 2,000 arrests.

The damage was spread across the country. The 143-year-old town hall in Limoges was set ablaze and its spire collapsed on camera, Marseille's city hall was broken into and defaced, Lyon's tourist office was torched, and shops were looted in Paris, where police fired tear gas at a smaller follow-on gathering at Place de la République on Sunday. The head of Carrefour said around 1,500 of the retailer's stores nationwide were affected.

Macron tried to split the crowd in two: he said those who destroyed and looted would be made to pay, while insisting the government should listen to the grievances of the hundreds of thousands who marched peacefully. He has asked his government to bring students, teachers and trade unions together this week to work on concrete proposals.

That meeting is now the test. The student movement's demands — smaller classes, more school spending, buildings that can handle a warming climate — predate the riots, and talks with the education minister have so far produced no agreement. If this week's session also stalls, organizers have already shown they can put half a million people back on the street.

items.title: Four Canadian service members killed, 39 hurt in fire at Alberta military base
items.summary:
Four Canadian service members were killed and 39 others are in hospital after a fast-moving fire swept through Canadian Forces Base Wainwright in Alberta on Saturday afternoon while soldiers were training on the range. Prime Minister Mark Carney confirmed the deaths on Sunday, calling it one of the worst peacetime tragedies for the armed forces on Canadian soil, and ordered flags on federal buildings lowered to half-mast. Alberta Premier Danielle Smith said at least 19 of the injured are in critical condition.

The fire started inside the base's training area and spread rapidly beyond it in high winds, according to the Canadian Armed Forces. Wainwright's own health facilities were quickly overwhelmed: Alberta declared a code orange, its protocol for mass-casualty events, and deployed 30 emergency units — ground ambulances plus fixed-wing and rotary aircraft — to move patients to hospitals in Wainwright, Edmonton, Red Deer and Calgary. The code orange was lifted by Sunday afternoon. Families of those killed have been notified; the dead and injured include reservists and members of Princess Patricia's Canadian Light Infantry.

What caused the fire is still unknown. A defence official told CBC there is no indication of terrorism, and no evacuation order was issued for surrounding residents, though people were asked to stay away and keep roads clear.

Investigators now have to reconstruct how a training exercise turned fatal at one of Canada's largest and busiest bases — home to the Canadian Manoeuvre Training Centre, about 210 kilometres southeast of Edmonton. Expect the inquiry to focus on the range exercise itself, the wind conditions, and how quickly the fire outran the base's own response.

items.title: U.S. resumes sharing missile-warning intelligence with Ukraine, Zelenskiy says
items.summary:
The United States has resumed giving Ukraine the critical intelligence it uses to defend against Russian missile strikes, President Volodymyr Zelenskiy said in comments published Sunday. Speaking to NBC's Meet the Press, Zelenskiy said the sharing had been interrupted but was later, in his word, "de-blocked," adding: "We are very thankful for this. Now it works."

The detail matters because of what the intelligence does. Ukraine relies on American data to spot fast-moving ballistic missiles that Russia fires in waves at its cities, and Ukrainian officials had said some recent strikes arrived without warning during the pause. President Trump had said earlier in the week that Washington was still sharing intelligence, a claim that sat awkwardly next to Kyiv's account until Zelenskiy's Sunday comments.

The resumption lands in a crowded diplomatic week. Zelenskiy also said Sunday he had spoken with U.S. envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner amid what he called virtually nonstop communication between the two teams about next steps, following a meeting in Florida.

For Kyiv, the practical question is durability: whether the restored flow stays on through the winter missile campaign, or whether it remains a lever Washington can pause again. For now, Ukrainian air defenders have their warning system back.

items.title: U.S. and EU condemn West Bank settler attacks after diplomats are targeted
items.summary:
American diplomats walked through the Christian Palestinian town of Taybeh in the occupied West Bank on Sunday, two days into a wave of settler attacks that has now drawn formal condemnation from both Washington and the European Union. The visit followed an attack Saturday on Belgian, French and Polish diplomats — along with a French mayor and Palestinian civilians — near the town, and the hospitalization Friday of Washington Post photojournalist Heidi Levine, who was assaulted while covering a Palestinian olive harvest near another village.

The EU's foreign policy spokesperson said Sunday the bloc "strongly condemns" attacks by violent settlers, including against European diplomats, and expects accountability and protection during the olive harvest and for journalists. France urged Israel to arrest Saturday's attackers. By Sunday, Israeli authorities had announced no arrests in either incident. Foreign Minister Gideon Saar and the Israeli military blamed "Israeli rioters," while Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu was more circumspect, saying the diplomats had entered a sensitive area without prior coordination and that the facts of the attack on Levine were unclear.

The numbers behind the weekend are stark: the Israeli human rights group Yesh Din counts at least 170 settler attacks since September 27, with journalists, activists and foreign observers increasingly among the targets, and prosecutions rare. On Sunday, Reuters journalists watched at least 10 masked settlers hurl rocks at Palestinians and activists harvesting olives near Salfit as border police fired tear gas toward the hills.

With about 500,000 settlers living alongside at least 3 million Palestinians in the West Bank, the attacks are becoming a diplomatic problem for Israel, not just a security one — especially in an election month, with the vote set for October 27.

items.title: Trump endorses Netanyahu nine days before Israel's election
items.summary:
President Donald Trump formally endorsed Benjamin Netanyahu on Sunday, nine days before Israelis vote in their first national election since the Hamas attack of October 7, 2023. In a Truth Social post addressed to the people of Israel, Trump called Netanyahu "Strong, Brave, and Brilliant" in the face of tremendous opposition and said the letter should serve as his "Complete and Total Endorsement" of Netanyahu's re-election as prime minister.

The timing is deliberate: Trump told Axios he "was always going to do that" and simply did not want to do it too soon. Netanyahu thanked him for the tremendous support. The vote on October 27 will decide whether Netanyahu stays in power after one of the most consequential periods in Israel's history — wars in Gaza, Lebanon and Iran — or is replaced by centrist rivals promising a new era. Polling has Netanyahu's Likud trailing Gadi Eisenkot's Yashar in several surveys, with no candidate holding a clear path to a coalition majority.

An American endorsement carries weight in Israel, but coalition arithmetic usually carries more. Even a strong Likud showing would still require Netanyahu to assemble partners, and his current coalition is projected to lose its governing majority.

Trump paired the endorsement with a warning to Iran to "change their ways, rapidly" or "we will soon finish the job" — a reminder that the U.S.-Israel conflict with Iran, now months old, hangs over the campaign's final stretch and could still reshape it.

items.title: Zelenskiy: Russia has hit Ukraine's energy sector 76 times since the announced ceasefire
items.summary:
Russia has attacked Ukraine's energy, oil and gas sectors 76 times in the week since President Trump announced a halt to attacks on energy infrastructure, President Volodymyr Zelenskiy said Sunday. The latest strikes hit substations in the Vinnytsia, Zhytomyr, Khmelnytskyi and Odesa regions — the kind of damage that translates directly into blackouts as temperatures fall.

Neither Kyiv nor Moscow has confirmed the ceasefire agreement Trump announced, and the gap between the announcement and the reality on the grid is becoming the story. Ukraine's foreign ministry added a separate embarrassment Sunday, saying it regretted the possible diversion of Ukrainian drones into Lithuanian airspace that morning — possibly caused by Russian electronic warfare during an operation against targets inside Russia — and apologizing to its Lithuanian partners.

The energy strikes also sharpen the fight in Washington over Trump's Friday decision to waive Russia sanctions, which Secretary of State Marco Rubio says the president will take up to 60 days to review. Zelenskiy has warned the waiver will embolden Moscow; 76 attacks in a week is his government's Exhibit A.

What to watch is whether the strike count changes the sanctions debate in Congress, and whether any verifiable energy ceasefire — with terms both sides actually acknowledge — emerges from the near-constant contact Zelenskiy described Sunday between Kyiv and Trump's envoys.

items.title: Rubio says Trump will take up to 60 days to weigh the Russia sanctions he waived
items.summary:
Secretary of State Marco Rubio says President Trump will take up to 60 days to assess the economic impact of the Russia sanctions and tariffs he waived on Friday, just before they were due to take effect. The waiver covers measures under the Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act — tariffs on Russian goods and penalties on countries that buy Russian oil and gas — and the order itself did not say how long it would last. Rubio's 60-day clock is the first timeline the administration has attached to it.

Rubio pointed to a genuine complication: the same law calls for tariffs on goods from countries that import Russian energy, including India, an important U.S. partner still heavily dependent on Russian oil. He also defended a separate deal under which Russia will initially supply more than 300,000 metric tons of diesel to the United States, arguing that diesel would be sold one way or the other — and that the wars in Ukraine and the Middle East are, in his words, starting to crash into each other on energy prices.

Congress is not waiting quietly. Sen. Thom Tillis called the waiver "beyond irresponsible," citing the Senate's 86-11 vote for the law; Sens. Chuck Schumer and Elizabeth Warren also attacked it, and a dozen senators signed a letter condemning it. Sen. Darline Graham of South Carolina, whose late brother Lindsey Graham championed the act, said she disagrees and would keep pressure on Russia. Sen. James Lankford defended the president on Meet the Press, and Trump himself argued on social media that easing sanctions gives him leverage in peace talks. Zelenskiy warned the move will embolden Putin.

The 60-day review runs straight through the November 3 midterms, which is why the fight matters beyond foreign policy: watch whether Congress tries to force the sanctions back on by legislation, or whether the review quietly becomes the policy.

items.title: Omar's lawyers demand the Justice Department return property seized from her home
items.summary:
Lawyers for Rep. Ilhan Omar sent federal prosecutors a letter late Friday demanding the immediate return of everything seized in this week's search of her Washington home, and challenging the search itself as unlawful. Homeland Security Investigations agents executed the warrant early Monday, taking her cellphone, notebooks, personal computers and passport, in an investigation focused at least in part on how Omar obtained her citizenship after arriving from Somalia decades ago.

The letter says there is no legitimate basis for any suggestion Omar violated citizenship law — her lawyers note she was lawfully naturalized in 2000 — and calls the investigation "vindictive, retributive, and politically motivated," aimed at one of the president's chief congressional critics. It also alleges procedural failures: that the House general counsel was not notified ahead of time as the magistrate instructed, that Omar was not given a copy of the warrant beforehand, and that agents kept her from contacting counsel for more than an hour. More than a dozen grand jury subpoenas have been issued, including to relatives in Washington and Minnesota.

The Justice Department pushed back hard. A spokeswoman called the letter "riddled with false allegations and inaccuracies" and said agents complied with all court orders; U.S. Attorney Jeanine Pirro noted a federal judge, conscious of Fourth Amendment rights, signed the warrant on probable cause. Former President Barack Obama weighed in Sunday, calling the probe political targeting.

The timing is the political flashpoint: the search came three weeks before midterms in which Omar is seeking a fifth term, and the Justice Department traditionally avoids public investigative steps involving candidates within 60 days of an election. Officials deny violating that policy. Expect the fight over the seized property — and over whether the warrant's conditions were followed — to play out in court filings next.

items.title: Katie Zacharia is out as White House press secretary after just five days
items.summary:
Katie Zacharia's tenure as White House press secretary lasted five days — the shortest for a modern-era press secretary, and less than half of Anthony Scaramucci's famous 11 days as communications director in President Trump's first term. Five sources familiar with the decision, including three senior White House officials, confirmed she is transitioning out after a rocky first briefing and questions about her credentials.

Her only briefing, on October 13, lasted about 14 minutes: she read prepared remarks and took questions from just three reporters, all from conservative outlets, and was widely panned as unprepared. Communications director Steven Cheung defended her the next day, saying she would be remembered as an all-time great — but by Thursday she was being grilled on air by Trump ally Sean Hannity, and it emerged that the Pepperdine law graduate had failed the California bar exam in 2011 and never obtained a U.S. law license despite publicly identifying as a lawyer. A watchdog group filed a bar complaint.

Trump told reporters Friday he had asked her to consider stepping down — "Honestly, if I were you, I'd reconsider" — while saying she had been treated roughly by the media. Zacharia, a former Fox News and Newsmax guest who worked for the company running Truth Social, posted that serving Trump was an honor.

No replacement has been announced. Axios reported Trump originally wanted Maria Bartiromo for the job and that she signaled she would not take it — leaving the White House without a chief spokesperson less than three weeks before the midterms, when it can least afford a communications vacuum.

items.title: New poll puts Trump at 36% approval, with voters preferring Democratic control of Congress
items.summary:
A new AP-NORC poll released heading into the final stretch of the midterms finds President Trump at 36% approval and 64% disapproval — matching a Fox News poll that Axios described as the lowest approval of either of his presidencies. Asked who should control Congress, voters preferred Democrats for the House by 47% to 38%, and for the Senate by 46% to 38%, with 15% unsure.

The issue numbers explain the mood. Eighty-five percent of voters call the economy a top issue and 84% say the same about the cost of living — and 74% disapprove of Trump's handling of the economy, rising to 79% on cost of living. His strongest listed issue is crime, at 45% approval. Health care ranks as a top issue for 69%, the war with Iran for 64%, and immigration and crime for 45% each. Eight in 10 voters say they want substantial change or complete upheaval in how the country is run; only 1 in 10 feels optimistic about American politics.

The poll interviewed 1,119 adults on the AmeriSpeak Panel from October 8–12, with a margin of sampling error of plus or minus 3.9 percentage points. Trump's favorable rating, 35%, matches Vice President JD Vance's; the Republican Party sits at 36% favorable versus 40% for Democrats.

Polls are snapshots, not results — but a 36% approval rating three weeks before a midterm is historically the kind of number that drags down a president's entire party, which is why both the House preference and the generic mood measures in this survey will get so much attention this week.

items.title: Anti-party, anti-politician candidates surge as the midterms enter the final stretch
items.summary:
The defining candidates of this midterm cycle may be the ones running against their own parties. Axios reported Sunday that in red states and blue states alike, unconventional candidates are downplaying — or outright disowning — party labels to tap into voters' deep disdain for Washington, arriving from pulpits, NFL sidelines and other places well outside the usual political pipeline.

The pattern shows up in the advertising. Axios's review of hundreds of ads across House, Senate and statewide races found Democratic ads attacking their own party, or both parties, as corrupt and ineffective have surged this cycle while positive party ads have plummeted. California Democrat Randy Villegas tells voters Washington is broken because corrupt politicians in both parties serve donors and party bosses; New York Democrat Blake Gendebien promises to stand up to anyone, Democrat or Republican; and Ohio's own Rep. Marcy Kaptur, a Democrat first elected decades ago, says Washington is "not just broken, it's deeply corrupt, and both parties need to shape up."

Axios's read is blunt: the outsiders might not all win, but the sheer number connecting with voters says something about an electorate that is angry and willing to take risks.

That mood lines up with the weekend's polling — a president at 36% approval and 8 in 10 voters wanting substantial change or upheaval. If anti-party candidates overperform on November 3, both parties' 2028 playbooks get rewritten around the same lesson: the label is a liability.

items.title: Axios: Some MAGA allies have discussed martial law if the midterms are deemed 'rigged'
items.summary:
Some of President Trump's MAGA allies have discussed extraordinary measures — including martial law — if they come to believe the midterm elections were rigged, according to Axios reporting that continued to circulate this weekend. The discussion traces to a September 30 video call on Rumble, where attorney Peter Ticktin, a childhood friend of Trump's, said there would have to be martial law in the event of another rigged election, and later told Axios that ballots and voting equipment would probably need to be commandeered.

Other participants pushed related ideas: former Colorado elections official Tina Peters has advocated hand-marked paper ballots and manual recounts, and activist Gregory Stenstrom has promoted pausing the election or invoking the National Emergencies Act. Axios noted that some of the proposals go far beyond the president's legal authority, and that there is no evidence the elections will be rigged. The White House has not endorsed any of the proposals.

Why the story matters is access. The people floating these ideas are not anonymous accounts — they have close access to the president, which makes their contingency talk a live political fact three weeks before voting ends, whatever its legal footing.

Watch for two things: whether the White House distances itself explicitly, and whether any of this language migrates from activist calls into official statements as results come in on November 3.

items.title: Anthropic commits 5% of its shares to a new public benefit fund
items.summary:
Anthropic said Sunday it will commit 5% of its shares to a new public benefit fund, subject to stockholder approval — an unusual move that ties a slice of one of the world's most valuable AI companies directly to societal-good spending. The fund is structured as a wholly owned entity within the company, and the stake can grow: Anthropic has the option to contribute an additional 2% for every 50% increase in its valuation.

The company was deliberately broad about what the money is for — possibilities it offered include large donations to traditional nonprofits or direct distributions to specific populations. Anthropic has already committed $200 million to study AI's impact on the job market, but said that given the pace of AI progress, bolder approaches may be needed, and that the fund gives it the versatility to pursue them.

The announcement is also reputation management. The AI industry faces increasingly negative public sentiment, which CEO Dario Amodei has described as fundamentally a crisis of trust. A permanent, equity-backed fund is a more durable answer than a one-off donation pledge — its budget grows automatically if Anthropic's valuation does.

What is missing is governance: Anthropic says details on the fund's structure and who decides what gets funded will come in the coming months. Until then, the commitment is real but its direction is unwritten.

items.title: Accenture looks to sell its Chinese operations for up to $1.5 billion, FT reports
items.summary:
Accenture is looking to sell its Chinese operations for up to $1.5 billion, the Financial Times reported Sunday, citing people familiar with the matter. The IT consulting giant has hired JPMorgan to run a strategic review of the business after receiving unsolicited interest in the unit over the past year. Reuters said it could not immediately verify the FT report, and neither Accenture nor JPMorgan commented outside regular business hours.

The unit on the table is bigger than "China" alone suggests: Accenture's Greater China operations span mainland China, Hong Kong and Taiwan, per the company's own website. The FT report says Accenture may retain a significant minority stake rather than exiting entirely, and that the process is likely to draw private equity groups and a small cluster of strategic buyers.

A sale would be one of the clearest corporate examples yet of Western firms restructuring around geopolitical friction — keeping a financial interest in the Chinese market while handing operational control to owners who face fewer political constraints on either side.

Context for the timing: Accenture recently forecast fiscal 2027 revenue growth of 3% to 6%, above analyst estimates, so this is not a distressed seller. Watch whether a buyer emerges at the reported price, and whether other multinationals with large China services arms follow the same minority-stake template.

items.title: AI rally wobbles as earnings week turns into a test for Meta and the chipmakers
items.summary:
The AI trade that has powered the stock market's bull run — which just marked its four-year anniversary — stumbled through last week, and now earnings have to bail it out. Semiconductor and tech hardware shares slid, Dell among them, and investors spent the week worrying about the debt financing the data-center build-out, particularly AI cloud firm CoreWeave and its roughly $50 billion in debt. Strategists at Deutsche Bank and RBC Capital Markets both pulled back on tech recommendations.

This week's results are the first real verdict. Meta, one of the hyperscalers spending massively on AI infrastructure, headlines the reports, with chipmakers Lam Research and Texas Instruments also reporting Wednesday, and Tesla, Netflix, Procter & Gamble and GE Aerospace on the calendar. The bar is high: S&P 500 companies are expected to post third-quarter earnings growth of more than 30%, and the five big AI hyperscalers are expected to lift capital spending to about $1.2 trillion next year, according to Goldman Sachs.

The damage so far is contained — the S&P 500 sits only about 1% below its record high from earlier this month, with other sectors picking up the slack, and the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index, down 8% this month, is still up more than 60% for the year. Hot inflation data, which has boosted bets on another Fed rate hike, is the other pressure on expensive growth stocks.

As one Natixis strategist put it, the market narrative feels jittery and there is a lot of uncertainty around where AI stands right now. This week's numbers — especially whether Meta's spending is producing revenue to match — will decide whether the wobble was a pause or a turn.

items.title: Rivian's next act: selling its tech to everyone else
items.summary:
Rivian CEO RJ Scaringe wants his company to be much more than an electric vehicle maker. In a TechCrunch Disrupt interview published Sunday, the word that kept coming up was "tech supplier": Rivian is clearing a path to license its electric architecture and software — and its AI models and autonomy stack — to many different brands, not just put them in its own trucks and SUVs.

The pieces are further along than the framing suggests. Rivian already has a $5.8 billion joint technology venture with Volkswagen Group covering electric architecture and software, and Scaringe talked about expanding it into AI and autonomy. The company is developing custom silicon — a 5-nanometre processor with Arm and TSMC — has built its own AI models for its in-vehicle assistant, and is working on an end-to-end automated driving stack for passenger cars and future robotaxis through a partnership with Uber.

Scaringe is spinning out adjacent businesses, too: industrial robotics startup Mind Robotics, which he founded, is now 31% owned by Rivian, counts former Ford, Apple and Tesla executive Doug Field as president, and plans to build robots for Rivian's factories and for other companies. A micromobility skunkworks program has already spun out as a separate startup called Also.

The strategy mirrors what the market rewarded in Tesla's software ambitions and what legacy automakers keep paying for: platforms scale better than vehicle margins. Whether licensing revenue can become a real second business — before the R2 and R3 launches decide Rivian's near-term fate — is the multi-year question Scaringe is now explicitly asking investors to judge him on.

items.title: Google now pays more than 400 publications to feed AI features in Google News
items.summary:
Google's paid news-for-AI pilot has grown past 400 publications worldwide, the company said in an October 15 announcement reported this weekend. The newest named partners include Axios, CNN, the Financial Times and Forbes, alongside local U.S. outlets such as the Texas Tribune, the Post and Courier, Oil City News and Shaw Media. The program launched last December with nine partners, including The Washington Post, The Guardian, Der Spiegel and El País.

The deal structure is licensing, not pay-per-use. Google pays participating publishers for the delivery and use of "enhanced content" to build AI features — the examples are in-depth article overviews on Google News publisher pages, offering context before a reader clicks, and customizable audio briefings. Both features carry clear attribution and direct links, Google says. A spokesperson clarified the pilot is not a pay-per-value model: publishers are not compensated based on how much their content contributes to AI outputs, and a separate program, covering about 100 publishers, handles AI Overviews, AI Mode and Gemini.

What Google did not disclose is the money — no amounts, terms, or country breakdown — so the size of these deals remains unknown even as the roster becomes a who's who of English-language news.

The expansion lands while publishers report steep declines in Google search referrals and regulators in the EU and UK examine how Google uses news content for AI. For newsrooms, the pilot poses the familiar bargain in a new form: paid licensing and attribution today, against the risk that AI summaries train readers not to click at all.

items.title: Trump says Washington golf course renovation will start November 15 despite a judge's order
items.summary:
President Trump said Sunday his administration will begin renovating the historic East Potomac Golf Links in Washington on November 15 and reopen it in about 15 months — announcing a start date for a project a federal judge has ordered cannot proceed without prior court notification. The Truth Social announcement sets up a direct test of U.S. District Judge Ana Reyes's authority over the project.

The court fight has been escalating for months. Reyes ruled earlier this year that the government must give notice before substantive construction. On October 9 the administration asked her to dismiss the underlying lawsuit — brought by the DC Preservation League in February over environmental and historic preservation concerns — as premature. The next day, the government removed about 500 trees from the site, saying it improved safety and restored the original design under a 2019 plan; Reyes halted further tree removal and called the move inexcusable. On Friday, the government moved to disqualify Reyes entirely, arguing her actions show deep-seated antipathy toward the administration.

The White House did not immediately respond Sunday when asked whether the November 15 start would conflict with the judge's directives. Trump had earlier said work would begin in September; the golf course is one of several Washington landmarks and spaces his administration is reshaping.

The next move belongs to the court: whether Reyes treats a public start-date announcement as defiance, and whether the disqualification motion changes the judge before the bulldozers are scheduled to arrive.

items.title: 'No Kings: Vote Early' rallies turn from protest to getting ballots cast
items.summary:
The No Kings movement changed its ask on Saturday: less marching against President Trump, more making a plan to vote. Hundreds of events under the banner "No Kings: Vote Early" were held in cities and communities across the country, billed as nonpartisan voter participation, with partner organizations including the ACLU and Common Cause. Organizers said the point was ensuring every eligible voter understands their options and has a plan to cast an early ballot before the November 3 midterms.

At the Lincoln Memorial, a band played for a few hundred people in caps and coats in chilly Washington weather, surrounded by signs reading "VOTE EARLY" and "HANDS OFF MY VOTE!" In Atlanta, City Councilman Michael Julian Bond urged the crowd to go urge others to vote, saying the Constitution gives the people that power. Organizers cited more than 3,000 events nationwide across the movement's planning.

The rallies played out against an escalating fight over the mechanics of voting itself. The administration sued California election officials Thursday, seeking to block counting of mail ballots from voters the federal government flags as likely noncitizens until status is confirmed, and on Friday the Justice Department warned local officials who process ballots by suspected noncitizen voters that they risk criminal investigation. Democratic senators wrote the attorney general the same day demanding a commitment that the department will not seize ballots or election materials before results are certified.

Polls suggest Democrats are positioned to retake the House while the Senate stays too close to call — which is exactly why both sides are fighting over who votes, how, and whether those ballots get counted.

items.title: Search continues for 11 missing after boat capsizes off Baja; survivors treated for shark bites
items.summary:
Eleven people are still missing after a boat capsized off Mexico's Baja California coast on Friday, in a rescue that has already pulled 16 people from the water — several of them suffering severe injuries consistent with shark bites. The U.S. Coast Guard said the vessel went down about 140 miles from Ensenada after a mayday call around 1 a.m., and that the search continues with help from the Mexican Navy.

Lt. Santiago Tamburini of the Coast Guard said it took 90 minutes to rescue the 16 survivors: "People were holding onto each other, to debris, just treading and trying to stay above water." Two survivors were reported in critical condition; the injured were given life-saving aid en route to hospitals in San Diego. All of those rescued are Mexican nationals, the Mexican consulate in San Diego told the Associated Press, and Customs and Border Protection officers are interviewing survivors, who have also been offered consular assistance.

Where the boat came from and where it was headed remain unknown. Capt. Robert Tucker of Coast Guard Sector San Diego said the vessel was heavily loaded and traveling a route normally used in illegal maritime smuggling operations — a corridor also used by fishing and leisure boats — though the capsizing did not occur in U.S. waters.

The case is a grim illustration of why that route is so dangerous: an overloaded boat, open ocean, and hours in the water. Whether the remaining 11 are found now depends on how long anyone can survive those conditions, and the search window narrows by the hour.

items.title: Hurricane center tracking storm-force low off the East Coast that could become a nor'easter
items.summary:
The National Hurricane Center is tracking a storm-force, non-tropical low expected to form off the Southeast coast later Sunday or tonight, in its 8 a.m. advisory. The system has a near-zero chance of subtropical development in the next 48 hours, but a 30% chance over seven days as it meanders slowly and erratically through the middle of the week near the warm waters of the Gulf Stream.

Development odds are almost beside the point for impacts. Regardless of whether it earns a name, the low is expected to bring high winds, coastal flooding and dangerous surf to stretches of the East Coast, with the most significant effects from North Carolina's Outer Banks through Delaware and into the mid-Atlantic and New England. Florida's east coast can expect heavy surf and rip currents, though the hurricane center says there is currently no tropical threat to Florida.

AccuWeather senior meteorologist Adam Douty noted that a storm lingering over the Gulf Stream can gradually pick up tropical or subtropical characteristics — but stressed the impacts would be the same either way. If it does develop, the next name on the 2026 Atlantic list is Josephine.

The season so far has produced nine named storms and one hurricane — Isaias, which came ashore near Destin on October 9 with 105-mph winds. With the season running through November 30, coastal residents from the Outer Banks northward should treat this week system as a nor'easter first and a naming question second.

items.title: Wichita driver released as police await toxicology and truck inspection after soccer tragedy
items.summary:
Wichita police released the 34-year-old driver whose pickup truck barreled onto a youth soccer field Saturday, killing a 6-year-old boy and a 35-year-old man and injuring 10 others, after interviewing more than 30 witnesses and consulting the district attorney's office. No charges have been filed. Police say the decision is explicitly pending two things: toxicology results and a mechanical examination of her Chevrolet pickup.

The truck had been parked in a space near the fields at the Stryker Sports Complex before it drove onto one of the fields around 3:25 p.m. Saturday. Two of the driver's own children were inside the truck and a third was playing soccer on a different field at the complex. Those killed — Cole Adrian, 6, and Nicholas Schafer, 35, both of McPherson and not related — were pronounced dead at the scene. The injured ranged from 5 to 68 years old, including five children; an 11th person was hospitalized for a medical condition unrelated to the crash. None of the injuries is believed to be life-threatening.

Police Chief Joe Sullivan captured the state of the case: investigators know what happened, but not yet why. The driver has been cooperative, and police have not made her name public.

That "why" is now the whole investigation — the toxicology and vehicle inspections will point toward medical or mechanical failure, impairment, or something intentional, and each path leads to a very different legal outcome. All events at the complex remain canceled while the community absorbs what Sullivan called a day that should have been children playing soccer and families spending time together, and ended in tragedy.

items.title: Browns stun Ravens 13-10 on Szmyt's walk-off kick, grab a share of first place
items.summary:
The Browns beat Baltimore 13-10 at Huntington Bank Field on Sunday in the most Cleveland way imaginable: Andre Szmyt missed a 48-yard field goal wide left with 3:40 to play, snapping his streak of 25 straight makes — then got a second chance in the final seconds when Baltimore was flagged offside on his blocked 42-yard try, and drilled the 37-yard walk-off as time expired. Cleveland, which trailed 10-0 at halftime with just 46 total yards, is 4-2 and tied for first in the AFC North.

The comeback turned on defense. Carson Schwesinger stripped Derrick Henry in the fourth quarter — his second straight game forcing a fumble the Browns recovered, on a 13-tackle afternoon — and Tyson Campbell's recovery at the Baltimore 35 set up a 2-yard touchdown by Audric Estime, signed off Minnesota's practice squad this week because Quinshon Judkins was out. Deshaun Watson's 33-yard strike to Jerry Jeudy on third-and-5 in the final two minutes moved Cleveland into range for the winner. Henry finished with 58 yards; Tyler Huntley, starting again for the injured Lamar Jackson, threw Baltimore's only touchdown, and the Ravens went scoreless for the final three quarters.

The stakes are real even if the style points are not. A share of first place this late in a season is a first for Cleveland since 2014, the Browns own the head-to-head tiebreaker and a 2-0 division record, and first-year coach Todd Monken beat the team he used to coordinate. Watson finished 16-of-26 for 164 yards and was sacked five times behind an offense that produced almost nothing for a half.

Next up is a trip to Tennessee next Sunday, October 25, followed by a visit to Pittsburgh on November 1 — two road games that will test whether a defense-and-kicker formula travels. Baltimore, also 4-2, hosts Cincinnati.

items.title: Rays lead Guardians 3-0 early in ALCS Game 5 as Messick's shortest start puts Cleveland in a hole
items.summary:
Game 5 of the American League Championship Series could hardly have started worse for Cleveland. Tampa Bay scored in each of the first three innings at Progressive Field on Sunday evening to lead 3-0, in a series tied 2-2 where the winner flies to Florida one win from the World Series. Parker Messick walked in a run with the bases loaded in a 31-pitch first inning, gave up an RBI single to Jonathan Aranda in the second, and was done after two innings — the shortest start of his career.

The line tells the workload story: Messick threw 57 pitches for six outs, allowing five hits and two walks, in a postseason in which his command has wobbled even as his regular season — 12-9 with a 2.56 ERA and 193 strikeouts — was ace-like. Tim Herrin took over in the third and immediately gave up a leadoff double to Chandler Simpson, who stole third and scored on Liam Hicks's RBI single. Meanwhile Drew Rasmussen held Cleveland to one hit through three innings.

Cleveland's path back runs through its bullpen, which must cover seven-plus innings — but it is the rested version: high-leverage arms Hunter Gaddis, Erik Sabrowski and closer Cade Smith all sat out Saturday's Game 4 blowout loss, a 7-3 Rays win that evened the series after Friday's rainout.

There is no recovery day coming. Game 6 is Monday night at 8 p.m. at Tropicana Field, and a Game 7, if needed, follows Tuesday — so every inning Cleveland's relievers burn tonight is borrowed from an elimination game tomorrow. Milwaukee awaits the winner in the World Series starting Friday; Cleveland has not won it since 1948, and Tampa Bay never has.

items.title: No. 4 Ohio State holds off No. 5 Indiana 19-15, but loses QB Julian Sayin for several weeks
items.summary:
No. 4 Ohio State survived the first top-five game ever played at Indiana's Memorial Stadium, beating No. 5 Indiana 19-15 on Saturday in a rematch of last December's Big Ten title game. The win moves the Buckeyes to 6-1 overall and 4-0 in the Big Ten, and it snapped Indiana's 22-game overall winning streak and 19-game home streak — both the longest active runs in the FBS, and coach Curt Cignetti's first home loss in three seasons.

Julian Sayin's 38-yard touchdown pass to Jeremiah Smith on fourth-and-1 early in the fourth quarter gave Ohio State a 19-7 cushion. Indiana clawed back behind Josh Hoover — a 19-yard touchdown to Nick Marsh plus a two-point conversion made it 19-15 with 10:30 left — and with 1:02 remaining, Hoover found Marsh wide open for what looked like the go-ahead score, only for it to be ruled incomplete because Marsh's left foot came down on the white paint out of bounds. Ohio State ran out the clock.

The victory came at a price. Sayin injured his right arm, left in the fourth quarter and was seen in a sling; coach Ryan Day said it looks like the quarterback will be out several weeks. Freshman Luke Fahey finished the game. Sayin finished 15-of-29 for 235 yards with two interceptions, his second straight week with multiple picks.

The bye week arrives at the perfect moment: Ohio State is off next weekend before visiting No. 19 USC on October 31, which gives Fahey a fortnight of first-team reps if Sayin cannot go. Indiana, now 6-1, travels to Michigan next weekend.

items.title: Obama to rally in Cleveland Oct. 24 for Acton and Brown as Ohio races tighten
items.summary:
Former President Barack Obama will come to Cleveland on Saturday, October 24, for a joint rally with the two Democrats at the top of Ohio's ballot: Dr. Amy Acton, running for governor against Vivek Ramaswamy, and former Sen. Sherrod Brown, running to unseat appointed Sen. Jon Husted. Early voting is already underway, and more than 170,000 Ohioans had cast ballots by late last week.

The location is the strategy. Democrats' Ohio problem is Greater Cleveland turnout: Cuyahoga County cast 667,000 ballots in 2008, when Obama first carried the state, and just 582,000 in 2024. The county's margins have decided Ohio before — Harry Truman carried the state by 7,000 votes in 1948 behind a 43,000-vote Cuyahoga margin, and Jimmy Carter by 11,000 in 1976 behind 96,000 in Cuyahoga. Acton and Brown both live in Bexley; their Republican opponents both live in Upper Arlington, a symmetry neither campaign is shy about mentioning.

The polling says the governor's race is genuinely competitive: YouGov and New York Times/Siena surveys both put Acton up 4, CNN put her up 8, and prediction market Kalshi had her around 68% in mid-October — despite Ramaswamy putting more than $36 million of his own money into the race, winning Trump's endorsement, and getting a Trump rally in Youngstown on October 12.

An Obama visit does not change a race by itself; it changes who shows up. If Cuyahoga turnout rebounds toward its old levels, Ohio flips from lean-Republican ground to a true battleground in both the governor's and Senate races — which is precisely the bet the rally represents.

items.title: Cleveland Hopkins unveils $3 billion master plan: two new concourses, 40 gates, rental cars back on site
items.summary:
Cleveland Hopkins International Airport has posted the full conceptual master plan for its $3 billion, two-decade rebuild — branded CLEvolution — and it is a wholesale reimagining of the airport rather than a facelift. The plan shrinks Hopkins from 46 active gates across three concourses to 40 gates across two brand-new concourses, roughly 20 gates each, built on either side of where Concourse B stands today. Every existing concourse, including the long-closed Concourse D, would eventually be demolished.

The most tangible change for travelers may be rental cars. A new consolidated rental facility on the Concourse D site would put rental counters within walking distance of the terminal for the first time since 1998; for 28 years, renters have shuttled across I-480 to Maplewood Avenue. The previously announced $1.6 billion first phase sits inside the larger plan: a new terminal headhouse, ground transportation center, parking garage and rail station. The $301 million transportation center was approved last month and is due by 2029, with the new terminal and roadways possible by 2032 and concourses following in 2033–2039.

Interest from builders is intense — the city hosted nearly 800 potential contractors at its CLEvolution Industry Day 2.0, for what Port Control Director Bryant Francis called the first major rebuild of Hopkins since the 1970s.

Two cautions come with the renderings: the plan is still conceptual and can shift with funding, the economy and the travel market, and the total estimate has already grown by about $1.4 billion from earlier figures. The airport Clevelanders use in the 2030s will look nothing like today's — if the money holds.

items.title: Cleveland moves to extend its data center moratorium into January 2027
items.summary:
Cleveland City Council is set to extend the city's data center moratorium — currently expiring October 20 — through January 29, 2027, meaning no new data centers will be entertained in Cleveland through all of 2026. The legislation, introduced last week, is led by Ward 13 Councilman Brian Kazy and Council's Data Center Working Group, which studied laws in other cities and held three town halls before concluding more work is needed.

Kazy's argument is sequencing, not opposition: residents want clear guidance on zoning, power grid impact and water usage first. "We want to make sure it's right. We don't want to rush it — in the meantime, the moratorium stays in place," he said. The bill heads to the Finance Committee next week, then the full Council, with a fuller package of data center legislation expected by the end of January.

Cleveland is not an outlier — it is part of a statewide wave. Ohio had 125 local data center moratoriums as of September; North Royalton, Kent and Grove City have passed bans, Grafton agreed a five-year pause, and 18 Ohio cities have data center bans on November ballots. The state already hosts 80 operating data centers with 189 more planned, clustered mostly around Columbus.

The local flashpoint is Lakeland Equity Group's proposed 150-megawatt hyperscale campus at East 55th Street — enough power for roughly 100,000 homes — which drew resident concerns about outages, bills and grid capacity at hearings. A state Joint Data Center Committee is meanwhile shaping House Bill 646, so Cleveland's January rules will land in the middle of a state-level fight, not settle one.
